findings.headline: CIPFA Bulletin 22 requires implementation of quinquennial revaluation or five-year rolling programme for property valuations from 2025/26.
findings.detail: From 2025/26, Authority must apply CIPFA Bulletin 22 which mandates quinquennial (five-year) revaluation or five-year rolling valuation programme for non-investment property assets, supported by annual indexation in intervening years. This represents change from prior annual revaluation requirement and requires careful management of valuation methodology.
findings.matters: Significant change to valuation methodology and frequency affects timing and basis of property asset valuations; requires careful selection of appropriate indices for years not subject to formal revaluation.
findings.figures: Five-year revaluation cycle requirement
findings.quote: The guidance mandates a quinquennial revaluation or a five-year rolling programme for formal valuations, supported by annual indexation in the intervening years.

findings.headline: Authority holds £46.4 million in long-term investments including £11.1 million in loans to subsidiary companies requiring impairment and recovery testing.
findings.detail: Balance sheet includes £46.4 million in long-term investments of which £11.1 million represents loans issued to subsidiary companies repayable over varying periods. Auditor will test assumptions and sensitivities used in impairment calculations and assess management's recoverability assessment against group performance.
findings.matters: Significant investment in subsidiaries, particularly loans, requires assurance over recovery risk and balance sheet valuation; material element of group financial position and potential exposure if subsidiaries underperform.
findings.figures: £46.4 million total long-term investments; £11.1 million subsidiary loans; investment balance £0.046 billion
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025 the Authority holds Long-Term Investments of £46.4 million in the Balance Sheet, of which £11.1 million relates to loans issued to subsidiary companies.

findings.headline: Building held by subsidiary reclassified from investment property to operational asset with upward valuation of £11.996 million in 2024/25.
findings.detail: University building held by Peterborough R&D Property Company was reclassified in group accounts from Investment Property at Fair Value to Property, Plant and Equipment at Depreciated Replacement Cost in 2024/25. The reclassification resulted in upward valuation of £11.996 million and recognition of accumulated depreciation of £0.542 million from 2021/22.
findings.matters: Step-change in valuation of material group asset affects group balance sheet position and indicates prior accounting treatment may not have captured true economic position; significant revaluation movements suggest asset base may have been understated.
findings.figures: Upward revaluation £11.996 million; accumulated depreciation £0.542 million from 2021/22
findings.quote: This reclassification has resulted in an upward valuation of £11.996 million and the recognition of accumulated depreciation of £0.542 million from 2021/22.

findings.headline: Three internal control recommendations from 2024/25 audit remain outstanding: journal authorisation, contract documentation, and loan agreements.
findings.detail: Auditor identified three control weaknesses in 2024/25 that remain unresolved: no formal procedure for authorising manual journals before posting to general ledger; contract variations not retained to support audit trail; loan facility agreements found undated and unsigned. All three will be followed up in 2025/26 audit.
findings.matters: Unresolved control deficiencies in journal authorisation, contracts, and loan agreements indicate gaps in financial oversight that increase risk of error or fraud in financial statements.
findings.figures: Three recommendations outstanding from prior audit
findings.quote: The Authority does not have any formal procedure for the authorisation of manual journals before they are posted to the General Ledger. This represents a level of weakness in the Authority's overall control environment and increases the potential risk of Management Override

findings.headline: Auditor expects limited assurance over opening balances at 1 April 2025 and closing reserves balance at 31 March 2026 due to continuing gaps in assurance.
findings.detail: Auditor anticipates limited assurance over opening balances and closing reserves for 2025/26 due to continuing lack of evidence over Pension Scheme Liability/Asset and Other Long-Term Liabilities. This is driving requirement for historic rebuild work on 2022/23 and earlier years. Key uncertainties remain unresolved from prior periods.
findings.matters: Reserve balances are critical to understanding a council's financial sustainability and ability to manage unexpected shocks; gaps in assurance prevent clear view of true financial position.
findings.figures: Year ended 31 March 2025; positions as at 1 April 2025 and 31 March 2026
findings.quote: As a result, we anticipate that for 2025/26: We will have limited assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26; and Limited assurance over the closing reserves balance, due to uncertainty over the opening amount.

findings.headline: Authority issued disclaimer opinions on financial statements for both 2023/24 and 2024/25 and expects limited assurance for 2025/26.
findings.detail: Auditor was unable to form an opinion on the Authority's financial statements in 2023/24 and 2024/25 due to application of the audit backstop, indicating material gaps in financial reporting arrangements. The Authority is following NAO recovery guidance with expected progression from disclaimer to qualified to eventually unqualified opinion over multiple years. For 2025/26, auditor anticipates limited assurance, continuing the multi-year rebuild process.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need assurance that a council's accounts are reliable; two consecutive disclaimer opinions indicate significant gaps in financial reporting and control environment.
findings.quote: In the audit reports for the years ended 31 March 2024 and 31 March 2025, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the application of the backstop. This means the auditor has not been able to form an opinion on the financial statements.

findings.headline: Integrated Settlement readiness assessment completed with gap analysis and work programme scoped
findings.detail: The Combined Authority completed an internal self-assessment and evidence-gathering exercise during 2025/26 against Integrated Settlement readiness criteria from MHCLG covering four capability areas (strategic planning, people and capability, financial and performance management, and reporting and evaluation). A gap analysis has been completed and a work programme to address identified gaps is being scoped for delivery.
findings.matters: Integrated Settlements are expected to bring additional devolved powers and funding to councils demonstrating readiness. Early preparation positions a council to access future funding and shows governance maturity.
findings.figures: Four capability areas assessed at four levels each; Core level considered ready for settlement
findings.quote: Following the initial self-assessment against the Integrated Settlement readiness criteria provided by MHCLG, the Combined Authority has completed a gap analysis and a work programme to address the gaps identified is being scoped and will be delivered to ensure that we can demonstrate that we achieve the required level of control maturity to support a future Integrated Settlement

findings.headline: Best Value Notice concluded following independent oversight completion
findings.detail: The Combined Authority's second Best Value Notice concluded in September 2024. The Independent Advisory and Support Group providing oversight concluded their support in June 2025. The Authority reports this signals recovery and that Best Value commitment is now embedded in regular governance processes.
findings.matters: Exit from Best Value Notice indicates a council has recovered from a period of governance or financial stress and returned to standard compliance status.
findings.figures: Second Best Value Notice concluded September 2024; oversight concluded June 2025
findings.quote: Following the conclusion of the second Best Value Notice in September 2024 the Combined Authority's Independent Advisory and Support Group concluded their support in June 2025, following the Mayoral election. This signals the Combined Authority's continued achievement of good governance and that this, along with the commitment to delivering Best Value, is now embedded within the foundations of the Combined Authority

findings.headline: £20 million annual funding granted over 30 years for regional investment
findings.detail: During 2025/26, the Combined Authority gained control of a £20 million annual funding allocation over 30 years for the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Single Investment Fund. This is one of several new devolved powers granted including adult skills provision, Local Growth Plan responsibilities, bus transport authority powers, and UK Shared Prosperity Fund delivery responsibilities.
findings.matters: This material new recurring funding stream significantly improves the council's financial resource base and is material to debt capacity assessment and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £20 million a year, over 30 years
findings.quote: Control of a £20 million a year funding allocation, over 30 years, to be invested in the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Single Investment Fund to boost growth.

findings.headline: External audit expected to progress from disclaimed opinion to qualified, then unqualified, over three years
findings.detail: The Combined Authority received disclaimed opinions on 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts due to national audit backstop delays affecting 44% of councils. Despite the disclaimer, auditors found no significant value for money weaknesses and rated the authority Effective on all 8 financial reporting areas assessed. The 2025/26 audit is expected to result in a qualified opinion, with return to unqualified opinion in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors track audit opinion as a key indicator of financial governance and statement credibility. Two years of disclaimed opinions is material; the documented recovery trajectory shows improving financial controls.
findings.figures: 44% of councils received disclaimed opinions; disclaimed 2022/23 and 2023/24; qualified expected 2025/26; unqualified expected 2026/27
findings.quote: the Combined Authority, along with 44% of all Local Authorities across the Country, received a disclaimed opinion on its 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts... the 2025/26 audit is expected to result in a qualified opinion rather than a disclaimer. This would represent a significant step forward... This should then set the groundwork for the 2026/27 accounts to return to complete 'unqualified' audit opinion.

findings.headline: 2026/27 treasury income expected to be lower than 2025/26 but exceed revised budget
findings.detail: The 2026/27 treasury income budget of £4.7m, set in January 2026, is expected to be exceeded but still not match the prior-year level of £9.8m. Market uncertainty and changing interest rate expectations are cited as factors affecting the projection.
findings.matters: Material anticipated decline in treasury income from prior-year levels signals reduced discretionary income available and requires budget planning adjustment.
findings.quote: Whilst the level of income in 2026/27 is not expected to match previous years it is anticipated to exceed the budget of £4.7m which was set in January 2026.

findings.headline: No breaches of prudential indicators during 2025/26
findings.detail: The council adhered to all agreed treasury and capital indicators throughout the year, confirming compliance with the prudential framework.
findings.matters: Compliance with prudential indicators is a statutory requirement and demonstrates prudent financial management and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: There have been no breaches of the agreed indicators during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Treasury management income delivered £9.8m against £5.6m original budget
findings.detail: The original budget of £5.6m was increased to £9.4m during the year as interest rates remained higher than forecast and expenditure was lower. The final outturn was £9.8m, representing significant outperformance.
findings.matters: Treasury income is discretionary and depends on investment decisions and market conditions; material overachievement supported the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £5.6m original budget, £9.4m revised budget, £9.8m outturn
findings.quote: The treasury management income budget for 2025/26 started as £5.6m. Due to a combination of lower than forecast expenditure and interest rates not falling as quickly as had been expected during the year due to 'sticky' inflation, this was increased to £9.4m through the 26/27 Medium-term financial plan and budgeting process, and the final outturn position was £9.8m.

findings.headline: No significant control issues identified for the Annual Governance Statement; five of seven core reviews returned positive or reasonable assurance opinions.
findings.detail: The internal audit concludes that no specific issues from 2025/26 work should be identified as significant control issues in the AGS. Five of seven core audit reviews returned positive assurance: Recruitment and Retention (Substantial Assurance), Payroll (Reasonable Assurance), Delivery of Transport Plan (Reasonable Assurance), Business Continuity (Reasonable Assurance), and Follow-up (Reasonable Progress).
findings.matters: An audit opinion with no material control weaknesses for the AGS is positive governance news; the prevalence of reasonable and substantial assurance opinions indicates that most core control areas are functioning adequately, which reassures lenders on the authority's governance baseline.
findings.figures: 1 Substantial Assurance, 4 Reasonable Assurance, 2 Partial Assurance, 2 Advisory opinions issued
findings.quote: In our view there were no specific issues identified as part of our Internal Audit work in 2025/26 that we believe should be identified as significant control issues within the Authority's AGS.

findings.headline: Audit and Governance Committee effectiveness review identified nine areas for consideration and potential enhancements.
findings.detail: An advisory review of AGC effectiveness, which plays a key role in the authority's governance arrangements, identified nine specific areas for consideration and potential enhancements. The specific areas are not detailed in this summary.
findings.matters: The AGC is responsible for oversight of internal controls and risk management; weaknesses in committee effectiveness could indicate governance gaps or reduced rigour in challenge and scrutiny.
findings.figures: nine areas for consideration and potential enhancements
findings.quote: We also undertook an advisory review of the AGC effectiveness, which plays an important role in the Governance arrangements. This identified nine areas for consideration and potential enhancements.

findings.headline: Follow-up audit found four of eight prior management actions fully implemented; three superseded with two weaknesses not addressed, and one not yet addressed.
findings.detail: The follow-up review of previously agreed management actions found positive progress but incomplete remediation. Four of eight prior actions have been fully implemented, three have been superseded, of which two had their underlying weaknesses not addressed before being replaced with new actions, and one action remains unaddressed.
findings.matters: Incomplete or delayed implementation of agreed audit actions indicates slower governance remediation and suggests control weaknesses may persist longer than intended, which affects the authority's risk position.
findings.figures: four of the eight actions have been fully implemented, 3 have been superseded with two of these weaknesses not addressed and superseded by new actions and one further action was not yet addressed
findings.quote: Overall, we found that four of the eight actions have been fully implemented, 3 have been superseded with two of these weaknesses not addressed and superseded by new actions and one further action was not yet addressed, demonstrating some progress in strengthening procurement and contract management controls but some issue remain to be addressed.

findings.headline: Advisory review of Key Financial Controls identified some control weaknesses in budget setting, forecasting, and financial performance.
findings.detail: A separate advisory review of Key Financial Controls covering budget setting, forecasting, and financial performance identified control weaknesses. The specific weaknesses are not detailed in this summary, though the review is noted as having six low-risk actions and one medium-risk action.
findings.matters: Budget setting and forecasting controls are fundamental to sound financial management and are core concerns for lenders assessing the authority's financial governance and ability to manage in-year financial performance.
findings.figures: 6 low-risk actions and 1 medium-risk action agreed
findings.quote: The Key Financial Controls review did identify some controls weakness which we have also detailed below.

findings.headline: Contract Management audit returned Partial Assurance due to inconsistent KPI monitoring and no centralised supplier performance oversight.
findings.detail: The authority has an established contract management framework with policies and templates, but weaknesses in implementation reduce effectiveness. Formal KPI monitoring and reporting was evidenced in only two of ten sampled contracts. No centralised oversight of supplier performance is in place, and a Contract Management Plan template has not yet been embedded in practice, though guidance is available.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the authority can monitor suppliers delivering services and achieving value for money; weaknesses in contract oversight affect the council's ability to manage procurement risk and ensure performance.
findings.figures: formal KPI monitoring and reporting evidenced in only two of the ten sampled contracts
findings.quote: weaknesses in implementation and consistency reduce its overall effectiveness. Key issues include inconsistent inclusion of KPIs and meeting requirements within contracts, and variation in how these requirements are applied and evidenced in practice.

findings.headline: Authority with £190.9m in treasury investments is shifting to internal borrowing model as capital spending depletes cash reserves
findings.detail: As at 31 December 2025, the Combined Authority held £190.9m in treasury investments earning 4.53% average return, with no external borrowing. However, it is 'expecting to become cash poor in the longer-term as capital expenditure is incurred before being financed'. Cash surpluses will be offset against capital shortfalls to reduce overall external borrowing need through internal borrowing.
findings.matters: Demonstrates how the authority will initially fund bus franchising without external debt markets; shows adequate cash buffer exists; explains the internal borrowing strategy; affects lenders' assessment of when external debt will actually be needed and at what levels
findings.figures: Treasury investments: £190.9m at average rate of 4.53%; expected to decline significantly as capital expenditure proceeds
findings.quote: The Authority has been cash rich in the short-term as grant income is received before it is spent but is expecting to become cash poor in the longer-term as capital expenditure is incurred before being financed. The cash surpluses will be offset against capital cash shortfalls to reduce overall borrowing.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure peaks at £96.20m in 2027/28 then declines to £60.95m by 2028/29
findings.detail: Total capital expenditure of £103.70m is planned for 2026/27, peaking at £96.20m in 2027/28 before declining sharply to £60.95m in 2028/29. Grant funding is reducing from £102.99m in 2025/26 to £58.17m by 2028/29, indicating end of current major grant programmes. Debt-financed bus franchising will represent an increasing proportion of total capital spend as external grants reduce.
findings.matters: Shows timing and scale of cash requirements; the 2027/28 peak requires significant funding to be in place; the subsequent reduction explains why borrowing is front-loaded; affects cash flow planning; lenders need to assess when revenue will be available to service debt

findings.headline: Annual financing costs will rise from £0.12m in 2026/27 to £2.57m by 2028/29, increasing from negligible to 3% of revenue stream
findings.detail: Current annual financing costs are £0.12m, representing less than 1% of net revenue. With bus franchising borrowing, costs reach £1.35m in 2027/28 (2% of revenue) and £2.57m in 2028/29 (3% of revenue). This represents more than a 20-fold increase over two years and will materially constrain revenue available for service delivery.
findings.matters: Shows the multi-year revenue consequences of borrowing decisions; constrains future spending flexibility on services; affects medium-term financial sustainability; finance directors need to understand how capital decisions create persistent revenue commitments
findings.figures: Financing costs: £0.12m (2026/27), £1.35m (2027/28), £2.57m (2028/29); as proportion of net revenue stream: 0%, 2%, 3%

findings.headline: Combined Authority plans to borrow £18.71m in 2026/27 to support bus franchising, with capital expenditure on the scheme rising to £39.66m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The Combined Authority has been debt-free but is planning its first material borrowing to support bus franchising following a mayoral decision taken on 7 February 2025. Capital expenditure on bus franchising is projected to grow from £18.71m in 2026/27 to £37.81m in 2027/28 and £39.66m in 2028/29. Internal borrowing is likely to be used initially rather than external debt.
findings.matters: This is a significant policy shift from a debt-free authority to one reliant on material borrowing; it affects creditworthiness, future financial flexibility, and borrowing capacity; lenders need to assess revenue implications; peer councils are watching how transport investment is being financed
findings.figures: Bus Franchising Capital Expenditure: £18.71m (2026/27), £37.81m (2027/28), £39.66m (2028/29); Capital Financing Requirement: £19.12m (2026/27), £38.10m (2027/28), £39.83m (2028/29)
findings.quote: The 26/27 MTFP contains plans to borrow to support Bus Franchising and the decision to formally start the process of Bus Franchising was taken by the previous Mayor on 7 February 2025

findings.headline: Authority has £84.61m authorized borrowing limit available despite forecasts not requiring near-term borrowing
findings.detail: While the authority does not currently expect to need to borrow based on capital funding forecasts, it retains legal authority to borrow up to £84.61m. This provides contingency headroom if the capital program timeline slips, costs increase, or if early long-term borrowing becomes cost-effective.
findings.matters: This shows the authority has options and flexibility if circumstances change, limiting downside risk to the capital program. A lender would see this as evidence of proper planning headroom.
findings.figures: Authorized borrowing limit: £84.61m; Current forecast borrowing requirement: £0m (internally funded)
findings.quote: The Authority may borrow to pre-fund future years' requirements, providing this does not exceed the authorised limit for borrowing of £84.61 million.

findings.headline: Investment income budgeted at £3.8 million for 2026/27 with no debt interest costs
findings.detail: The authority budgets for £3.8m of investment income in 2026/27 based on expected portfolio levels, with zero budget for debt interest. As investment holdings decline from £190.9m to £16.6m by 2029, this income stream will reduce, affecting both the revenue budget and the authority's ability to use investment yields to offset capital costs.
findings.matters: This shows the financial support investments currently provide to the revenue budget. Declining investment balances will reduce this income, potentially creating pressure on the revenue budget if not offset by other measures.
findings.figures: Investment income budget 2026/27: £3.8m; Debt interest budget 2026/27: £0m; Investment portfolio yield (31 Dec 2025): 4.53%
findings.quote: The budget for investment income in 2026/27 is £3.8 million, based on the expected investment portfolio at the time the MTFP was drafted. There is no budget for debt interest paid in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Bank Rate forecast to reach 3.25% in 2026 with strategy to use short-term borrowing or internal resources rather than long-term fixed borrowing
findings.detail: The authority's treasury adviser (Arlingclose) forecasts continued Bank Rate reductions to 3.25% in 2026, with long-term gilt yields remaining broadly stable but volatile. The authority's strategy is to prefer short-term borrowing or internal resources over long-term fixed borrowing while rates are expected to fall, though it will conduct cost-of-carry analysis to determine whether to lock in long-term rates in advance of future rate rises.
findings.matters: This explains why the authority is comfortable using reserves rather than borrowing now, but also indicates it will monitor whether early long-term borrowing becomes cost-effective as rates stabilize.
findings.figures: Bank Rate current 3.75% (Dec 2025), forecast 3.25% (2026); PWLB standard rate = Gilt yield + 1.00%
findings.quote: Arlingclose, the Authority's treasury management adviser, currently forecasts that the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee will continue to reduce Bank Rate in 2026, reaching around 3.25%.

findings.headline: Treasury investment holdings forecast to decline from £190.9m to £16.6m by March 2029
findings.detail: The authority's investment portfolio is expected to decrease sharply from current levels as capital funding is drawn down to finance capital expenditure and reserves are used to support the revenue budget. This constrains the current strategy of internal borrowing: the authority can only fund capital this way for as long as investment balances remain positive.
findings.matters: The sustainability of the debt-free strategy depends on this cashflow forecast. A lender would want to understand the timing of when the authority may need to borrow; a peer council would want to know the implications for investment income and financial resilience.
findings.figures: Investments: £190.9m (31 Dec 2025) declining to £16.6m (31 Mar 2029)
findings.quote: Investments are forecast to fall from current levels (end of Dec 2025) of £190.9m to £16.6m (end Mar 2029) as capital funding is used to finance capital expenditure and reserves are used to finance the revenue budget

findings.headline: Authority holds no borrowing as of 31 December 2025 with plans to fund capital expenditure for bus franchising from treasury investment holdings
findings.detail: The Combined Authority is currently debt-free with zero external borrowing. It plans capital expenditure for bus franchising estimated to create a Capital Financing Requirement of £18.7m–£39.7m between 2027 and 2029. This capital program is forecast to be fully covered by internal borrowing, meaning the authority will finance capital from its existing investment holdings rather than from market borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when the authority will become a borrower and on what timescale; a peer council would want to know whether this debt-free strategy is replicable elsewhere.
findings.quote: The borrowing related to bus franchising is fully funded over the life of the business case and is currently forecast to be fully covered by internal borrowing.

findings.headline: Lease capital financing requirement of £532k results in MRP charge of £122k for 2026/27 under IFRS 16 accounting
findings.detail: The adoption of IFRS 16 Leases has brought former operating leases onto the balance sheet. The resulting lease CFR of £532k will generate an MRP charge of £122k in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of all the council's payment obligations, including lease liabilities and the provisions being made for them.
findings.figures: £532k lease CFR, £122k MRP
findings.quote: The lease CFR is expected to be £532k on 31st March 2026 and MRP for 2026/27 is expected to be £122k.

findings.headline: Loans capital financing requirement expected to be nil on 31 March 2026, resulting in no MRP charge on debt for 2026/27
findings.detail: The authority expects no outstanding debt by 31 March 2026 and will charge no MRP on debt in 2026/27 in line with MHCLG Guidance. This represents the strongest borrowing position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt repayment obligations and all funded liabilities; nil debt means no annual repayment charge.
findings.figures: nil CFR on 31st March 2026
findings.quote: The Authority expects that its loans capital financing requirement will be nil on 31st March 2026 and in line with the MHCLG Guidance it expects to charge no MRP in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Final accounts A&G covering report Nov 2025
findings.headline: Peterborough R&D Property Company building to be reclassified from investment property to operational property; valuation change assessed as not material
findings.detail: The building held by Peterborough R&D Property Company (carrying amount £2.954m) will be reclassified from Investment Property to operational Property, Plant and Equipment in group consolidated accounts, with valuation basis changing from Fair Value to Existing Use Value. New valuations have been commissioned for three years. The initial March 2025 valuation indicates the change in value is not material. The adjustment affects group accounts only, not single entity accounts.
findings.matters: It represents an outstanding matter requiring final adjustment to the accounts prior to publication, though the immaterial assessment indicates no significant revaluation impact.
findings.figures: £2.954m carrying amount
findings.quote: At the time of publication, the 31 st March 2025 valuation has been received from the valuers which indicates the change in value from the reclassification is not material.

findings.paper_title: Final accounts A&G covering report Nov 2025
findings.headline: E-MSA status requires material accounting concerns to be resolved; authority clarifies disclaimed opinion does not itself indicate such concerns
findings.detail: Established Mayoral Strategic Authority status requires no material accounting concerns relating to ability to manage public money. A disclaimed opinion will likely persist until the national audit backlog is cleared. However, the authority clarifies that a disclaimed opinion caused by systemic backstop dates does not itself indicate material accounting concerns. The government's July 2024 Written Ministerial Statement stated authorities should not be unfairly judged based on disclaimed or modified opinions caused by factors beyond their control.
findings.matters: It flags a potential strategic constraint while clarifying the distinction between a systemic audit backlog issue and actual identified accounting weaknesses.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: a disclaimed opinion for an Authority's accounts will be likely remain until the audit backlog is cleared. However, a disclaimed opinion at this stage does not in itself indicate material accounting concerns.

findings.paper_title: Final accounts A&G covering report Nov 2025
findings.headline: No identified shortcomings or inaccuracies in accounts despite disclaimed audit opinion
findings.detail: The Combined Authority states explicitly that the disclaimed audit opinion does not indicate any identified shortcomings or inaccuracies in the 2024/25 accounts themselves. The disclaimer results from lack of assurance on opening balances due to the 2022/23 disclaimer, rather than defects found in the authority's financial statements. The draft accounts were published on schedule on 30 June 2025.
findings.matters: Lenders and other stakeholders may misinterpret a disclaimed opinion as signifying problems discovered; this explicit statement is important to understanding the underlying position.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: the disclaimed opinion being issued does not indicate any identified shortcomings or inaccuracies in the Combined Authority's accounts, nor any undue delay to the draft accounts being available for audit as the Combined Authority published these in draft on 30 June 2025.

findings.paper_title: Final accounts A&G covering report Nov 2025
findings.headline: Auditor expects qualified opinion in 2025/26 and unqualified opinion possible in 2026/27; authority working to accelerate timeline
findings.detail: EY's draft report indicates assurance will continue improving for the 2025/26 audit, resulting in a qualified opinion (representing greater assurance than a disclaimed opinion), with an unqualified opinion possible by 2026/27. The Combined Authority is actively exploring with its auditors whether this trajectory can be accelerated given the relative simplicity of its accounts structure.
findings.matters: Other finance directors managing the same systemic audit backlog need to see realistic timelines for resolution; lenders need visibility on when full audit assurance will be restored.
findings.figures: Qualified opinion expected 2025/26; unqualified opinion possible 2026/27
findings.quote: The Auditor's draft report indicates that they anticipate that assurance will improve again in 25/26, but still result in a qualified opinion, which indicates a greater level of assurance than the 24/25 accounts' disclaimed audit, with a return to an unqualified opinion being possible for the 26/27 accounts.

findings.paper_title: Final accounts A&G covering report Nov 2025
findings.headline: 2024/25 accounts to receive disclaimed audit opinion; assurance improved with 17 of 21 areas at substantial level against 7 of 21 in 2023/24
findings.detail: The Combined Authority will receive a disclaimed audit opinion for 2024/25, continuing from 2022/23 and 2023/24 due to the national local government audit backlog and backstop dates. However, assurance is strengthening: 17 out of 21 audit assurance areas now have substantial assurance, up from only 7 out of 21 in the previous year. This shows the impact of the opening balance lack of assurance is reducing.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need to understand whether accounts can be relied on; the improving assurance trajectory indicates the audit position is moving toward resolution despite the continued disclaimed opinion.
findings.figures: 17 out of 21 areas with substantial assurance (2024/25); 7 out of 21 (2023/24)
findings.quote: For the same reasons the 2024/25 will also have disclaimed opinion, but the impact of the lack of the assurance over the 22/23 closing balances is reduced as can be seen from the 'Summary of Assurances' table on p48-9 on EYs report with 17 out of 21 areas now having substantial assurance up from only 7 out of 21 for the 2023/24 audit.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Combined Authority - Audit Results Report - 29 October 2025
findings.headline: Pension asset/liability valuation work outstanding; Cambridgeshire Pension Fund auditor report expected 10 November 2025
findings.detail: The auditors' work on the Authority's pension asset/liability remains incomplete pending the report from Cambridgeshire Pension Fund's auditor, expected 10 November 2025. As at 31 March 2025, the Authority's share of the pension asset totals £0 due to the effect of the pension asset ceiling, but this significant accounting judgement requires assurance from the fund auditor before the audit can be finalised.
findings.matters: Pension valuations are material to the balance sheet and involve significant actuarial estimation; the outstanding assurance means the audit cannot be completed until the fund auditor's work is received.
findings.figures: £0 (recorded pension asset due to asset ceiling); report expected 10 November 2025
findings.quote: As of the date of this report, our work in this area remains outstanding. We are currently awaiting the assurance reporting from the Cambridgeshire Pension Fund auditor. The Pension Fund auditor has indicated that their report will be provided to us on 10 November 2025.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Combined Authority - Audit Results Report - 29 October 2025
findings.headline: £5.934 million reclassified from Long-Term to Short-Term Capital Grants Receipts In Advance
findings.detail: Audit procedures identified that £5.934 million should be reclassified from Long-Term Capital Grants Receipts In Advance to Short-Term Capital Grants Receipts In Advance, indicating that the timing of recognition was initially incorrectly classified. This reclassification misstatement has been corrected by management.
findings.matters: This misclassification affects balance sheet presentation and liquidity analysis; it also contributes to evidence gaps that led to the disclaimer, indicating control weaknesses in grant accounting.
findings.figures: £5.934 million reclassified
findings.quote: Balance Sheet – Capital Grant Receipts in Advance: Our audit procedures identified a reclassification difference between Long-Term Capital Grants Receipts In Advance to Short Term Capital Grants Receipts In Advance of £5.934 million

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Combined Authority - Audit Results Report - 29 October 2025
findings.headline: Two capital grant claim forms identified with expenditure dated before 2024/25 financial year
findings.detail: During testing of REFCUS expenditure (£87.795 million for 2024/25), auditors identified two claim forms submitted by third parties that pertained to expenditure incurred prior to 1 April 2024. The Authority was unaware the work had been completed before the financial year start. Auditors recommend the Authority enhance monitoring of multi-year projects to ensure grant income is recognised in the appropriate accounting period.
findings.matters: Capital grant income recognised in the wrong accounting period distorts annual financial position and affects budget planning; it indicates monitoring gaps in multi-year capital projects.
findings.figures: £87.795 million (total REFCUS expenditure 2024/25); 2 claim forms identified
findings.quote: During our testing, we identified two claim forms submitted by third parties that pertained to expenditure incurred prior to the 2024/25 period. These instances appeared to involve the initial grant claim submissions from the respective third parties, and the Authority was unaware of any work completed before the 1 April 2024.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Combined Authority - Audit Results Report - 29 October 2025
findings.headline: £2.306 million upward adjustment to Long-Term Investments in subsidiaries following audit procedures
findings.detail: Audit procedures identified that the valuation of Long-Term Investments in Subsidiaries was understated by £2.306 million to reflect the actual financial position of subsidiary companies as at 31 March 2025. This factual misstatement has been corrected by management in the revised financial statements.
findings.matters: The adjustment indicates the initial valuation process did not fully capture subsidiary financial position; for an authority with complex subsidiary structures including property companies, this raises questions about the adequacy of initial valuation procedures.
findings.figures: £2.306 million adjustment; total Long-Term Investments £46.1 million (£11.0 million in subsidiaries)
findings.quote: Our audit procedures identified net audit adjustments of £2.306 million relation to an increase in the valuation of 'Long-Term Investments in Subsidiaries' for the actual financial position of the subsidiaries as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Combined Authority - Audit Results Report - 29 October 2025
findings.headline: Some Loan Facility Agreements found undated and unsigned by either party
findings.detail: During audit testing, auditors identified that some Loan Facility Agreements were undated and unsigned by either party, indicating a control weakness in the loan approval process. The auditors recommend the Authority implement controls to ensure all loan agreements are properly dated and signed by both parties to confirm mutual acknowledgement and enforceability.
findings.matters: For a Combined Authority with borrowing relationships, undated and unsigned loan agreements create legal and financial risk and suggest inadequate controls over the approval and documentation of loans.
findings.figures: No specific count; identified as control weakness
findings.quote: Some Loan Facility Agreements were found to be undated and unsigned by either party, indicating a control weakness in the loan approval process.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Combined Authority - Audit Results Report - 29 October 2025
findings.headline: Authority lacks formal procedure for authorising manual journals before posting to General Ledger
findings.detail: The auditors identified that the Authority has no formal control procedure requiring authorisation of manual journals before they are posted to the General Ledger. While the auditors found no instances of actual management override, they have raised this as a control weakness that increases the potential risk of fraud or error.
findings.matters: Manual journal authorisation is a fundamental control; its absence suggests broader control environment weaknesses and increases fraud risk, particularly relevant to any stakeholder relying on financial data accuracy.
findings.figures: No specific figure; control finding
findings.quote: The Authority does not have any formal procedure in place for the authorisation of journals before they are posted to the General Ledger. Whilst we have raised this as a control weakness, we have not identified any instances where this has led to management override.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Combined Authority - Audit Results Report - 29 October 2025
findings.headline: Auditors disclaim opinion on 2024/25 financial statements for third consecutive year; unable to assure £17.912 million in Long-Term Grants Received in Advance
findings.detail: Following disclaimers in 2022/23 and 2023/24, the auditors are unable to express an opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. They lack sufficient audit evidence over the valuation of Long-Term Grants Received in Advance (£17.912 million), its impact on the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement, and the classification of Usable and Unusable Reserves. The backstop audit completion date of 27 February 2026 has constrained the scope of audit work available to rebuild assurance following the prior-year disclaimers.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years of disclaimer means the financial statements cannot be relied upon for decision-making or lending purposes, and indicates a systemic issue in either financial reporting or audit evidence gathering that undermines stakeholder confidence.
findings.figures: £17.912 million (Long-Term Grants Received in Advance); backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: As a result of the disclaimer of opinion on the 2023/24 financial statements, we do not have assurance over some brought forward balances from 2023/24 where we did not gain assurance (the opening balances). This means we do not have assurance over all 2024/25 in-year movements and the comparative prior year movements.

findings.headline: Five risks identified above the authority's risk appetite, including new fraud risk following audit committee recommendation
findings.detail: The October 2025 Corporate Risk Register contains 17 risks: 1 red very high, 4 amber high, 6 yellow medium, and 6 green low. Five are above appetite: future funding uncertainty, ability to deliver government devolution agenda, cyber security, bus reform programme delivery, and fraud. A fraud risk was newly added following steering from the Audit and Governance Committee.
findings.matters: Multiple risks above appetite threshold indicates heightened governance and operational pressure; new fraud risk addition reflects emerging control concerns identified by the audit committee.
findings.figures: 5 risks above appetite out of 17 total; 1 red, 4 amber, 6 yellow, 6 green
findings.quote: There are 5 above risk appetite: • Future funding uncertainty and impact on financial planning • Ability to deliver the Government's devolution agenda for Mayoral Strategic Authorities • Cyber Security and risk of access to sensitive information and/or disruption of operations • The Bus Reform Programme may not be delivered in line with Mayoral decision of 2025 • Fraud occurring in CPCA

findings.headline: Future funding uncertainty and impact on financial planning is rated red very high risk and above risk appetite
findings.detail: The risk has been identified since March 2022. It is rated 5/5 critical impact and 3/5 possible likelihood, even after controls are in place. The target score is to reduce impact to 4/5 and likelihood to 2/5, but this has not yet been achieved. The risk remains above the authority's risk appetite.
findings.matters: A persistent, critical funding uncertainty that cannot be mitigated to appetite level is material to anyone lending to or funding the authority, indicating unresolved challenges to financial planning and service delivery.
findings.figures: 5/5 critical impact, 3/5 possible likelihood (residual score), identified March 2022, target 4/5 impact and 2/5 likelihood
findings.quote: The risk was first identified in March 2022. The inherent risk score was very high with a 5/5 Critical impact and 5/5 Almost Certain likelihood. The residual score (now that controls are in place) is a very high risk, with a 5/5 Critical impact and 3/5 possible likelihood. The target score is to reduce the impact to 4/5 and likelihood to 2/5. This risk is above appetite.

news_drafts.headline: CIPFA Bulletin 22 requires implementation of quinquennial revaluation or five-year rolling programme for property valuations from 2025/26.
news_drafts.lead: Significant change to valuation methodology and frequency affects timing and basis of property asset valuations; requires careful selection of appropriate indices for years not subject to formal revaluation.

news_drafts.headline: Authority holds £46.4 million in long-term investments including £11.1 million in loans to subsidiary companies requiring impairment and recovery testing.
news_drafts.lead: Significant investment in subsidiaries, particularly loans, requires assurance over recovery risk and balance sheet valuation; material element of group financial position and potential exposure if subsidiaries underperform.

news_drafts.headline: Building held by subsidiary reclassified from investment property to operational asset with upward valuation of £11.996 million in 2024/25.
news_drafts.lead: Step-change in valuation of material group asset affects group balance sheet position and indicates prior accounting treatment may not have captured true economic position; significant revaluation movements suggest asset base may have been understated.
